Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Kai, a 39-year-old airline pilot of Pacific Islander heritage, could not have predicted that a routine traffic stop two years ago would unravel his life. He was pulled over for a broken taillight, but the encounter escalated within seconds. The officer shouted, ordered him out, and when Kai fumbled with his seatbelt, two more officers pinned him to the ground. His face pressed against the asphalt, one knee grinding into his back, he felt a wave of nausea rise from the struggle and the claustrophobic weight of bodies against him. The terror he felt in that moment-the certainty that he might not survive-never fully left him. When he was finally released without charges, he tried to convince himself it was over, but the memory refused to fade; it remained more vivid than ordinary recollections, so extreme that sometimes he caught himself doubting it had really happened.

In the months that followed, Kai found himself reacting to situations that had never bothered him before. As a pilot, he was accustomed to close quarters with colleagues in the cockpit, but now physical proximity-a hand on his shoulder, a passenger brushing past in the aisle-made his stomach drop and his heart race. Driving with friends or family became unbearable; he would cancel plans last minute rather than sit in a car with others, certain that any unexpected movement would trigger another confrontation. The nausea that had accompanied the assault began to surface unpredictably, and each time it did, he felt the same helpless dread. These triggers did not just cause discomfort-they actively generated threat. When someone approached him unexpectedly at the airport, he would startle, feeling a surge of adrenaline as if a stranger were a potential attacker. Delays, common in aviation, now felt ominous; if a flight was held on the tarmac, he assumed something bad was happening, scanning the cabin for signs of danger.

The connection between threat and memory tightened into a vicious loop. A sudden sound-a car backfiring, a door slamming-would make Kai jump, and in that flash of startle, the memory of the officers' shouts and the weight on his back would return with the same visceral terror. The more threatened he felt, the more often the memory intruded, and the more vivid and real it became. At the same time, the memory itself acted as a trigger: a single involuntary flashback could send him into a state of hypervigilance, his eyes darting at every passenger, his skin prickling at the thought of anyone standing too close. He began to believe that his environment was fundamentally unsafe. The threat-scanning never stopped, and it made him acutely aware of every potential trigger-so much so that he started avoiding the crew lounge, preferring to stay isolated before flights, and he became short with colleagues who asked too many questions. His marriage, already strained, could not survive his constant wariness and irritability; his wife left him six months ago, citing his emotional distance and unexplained absences.

It was a recent incident that finally drove Kai to seek help. During a cross-country flight, mild turbulence caused a wave of nausea strong enough that he had to focus intensely on his instruments to avoid a full panic attack. The memory of the police encounter broke through so vividly that he momentarily lost track of altitude. After landing, he sat in the cockpit for twenty minutes, trembling. What frightened him most was not the nausea or the startle-it was the growing certainty that his job, the one thing that had given him structure after the divorce, was becoming impossible to manage. He came to therapy hoping to understand why his mind kept pulling him back to that asphalt parking lot, and whether he could ever trust a stranger-or himself-again.
